quote: d.h. obige Gl. 6ten Grades ist irreducibel auch wenn man beliebig Gl. mit nur 2 Param. adjungirt d.h. [-auch-][?] in einem Rationalitätsbereiche wo alle Funktion von Funktion von Funkt. von 2 Argument enthalten sind.
english: i.e. the above equation of degree 6 is irreducible even if one adjoins arbitrary equations with only 2 parameters, i.e. in a domain of rationality where all functions of functions of functions of 2 arguments are contained.
topic: Hilbert discusses which functions of three variables can be built by successive composition of functions of two arguments, and proposes the root t of t^6 + x t^3 + y t^2 + z t + 1 = 0 as probably the simplest example of a genuine function of three variables, noting that a proof would likely be very hard.

triage.modern_statement: Take the algebraic function t(x,y,z) defined by t^6 + x t^3 + y t^2 + z t + 1 = 0. The conjecture is that this equation stays irreducible over every field obtained from C(x,y,z) by adjoining roots of algebraic equations whose coefficients depend on at most 2 parameters, including iterated (nested) adjunctions. Put another way, t cannot be written as a finite composition of algebraic functions of two variables, so its resolvent degree would be 3. The diary note is an early version, using a degree-6 equation, of what became Hilbert's 13th problem in 1900. The 13th problem asks the same question for f^7 + x f^3 + y f^2 + z f + 1 = 0.
triage.answered_by: As stated for degree 6, the conjecture is refuted by a classical result: W. R. Hamilton showed RD(6) ≤ 2, and A. Wiman and others later worked on this. The general sextic can therefore be solved with algebraic functions of at most 2 variables. The sextic in the note is a specialization of the general sextic, so its root is also reachable this way, and the 'irreducible after any 2-parameter adjunction' claim fails. This consequence is my own deduction from the published bound; I found no source that discusses this diary entry directly. For continuous functions, the Kolmogorov–Arnold theorem (Arnold, 1957) shows that every continuous function of 3 variables is a superposition of continuous functions of 2 variables. Hilbert's published 1900 problem uses degree 7 instead, and its algebraic version is still open. Hilbert's separate 1927 'Sextic Conjecture' (RD(6) = 2, i.e. the bound ≤2 is sharp) is also still open.

evidence.claim: Hamilton proved RD(6) ≤ 2, RD(7) ≤ 3 and RD(8) ≤ 4. Hilbert's sextic conjecture, the 13th problem and the octic conjecture predict that these upper bounds are sharp.
RD(n) is the minimum d such that the general degree-n polynomial can be solved by a formula in algebraic functions of at most d variables.
Hilbert's Sextic Conjecture (Hilbert 1927, p. 247) says the resolvent degree of the general sextic equals 2. Farb and Wolfson discuss this together with the 13th problem and the octic conjecture.
The 13th problem in the 1900 list uses the seventh-degree equation f^7 + xf^3 + yf^2 + zf + 1 = 0 and asks whether it can be solved using functions of two arguments.
Arnold settled the continuous variant in 1957 (Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem). The algebraic variant is still unresolved.
There are currently no non-trivial lower bounds on RD(n).
Farb and Wolfson have recently revived research on resolvent degree as the algebraic form of Hilbert's 13th problem.

triage.why: The note is clearly the sextic forerunner of Hilbert's 13th problem: same coefficient pattern and same 'functions of two arguments' framing. Read literally in the algebraic sense, it claims the root needs 3 parameters. That contradicts the classical bound RD(6) ≤ 2 attributed to Hamilton: any specialization of the general sextic, including this one, has resolvent degree at most 2. This may be why Hilbert's published 1900 problem uses degree 7. The continuous reading is refuted by Kolmogorov–Arnold. What remains open, and actively studied (Farb–Kisin–Wolfson, Sutherland), is the degree-7 algebraic 13th problem and the sharpness question RD(6) = 2. Confidence is medium for three reasons: no source discusses this diary entry directly; applying the RD(6) ≤ 2 bound to this particular sextic is my own (standard) deduction; and Sutherland notes gaps in some classical proofs (Wiman, Chebotarev), though the RD(6) ≤ 2 bound itself is restated in modern work.
